questions.title: How can a court rely on ex parte declarations in FOIA cases without violating due process?
questions.question_body: I'm confused by the procedural aspect of this case. The FBI submitted declarations 'ex parte' and 'under seal,' meaning the plaintiff, Farahi, never saw the specific evidence the court used to grant summary judgment. In any other area of law, I thought the opposing party had a right to see the evidence against them. Is this standard for FOIA cases, and how does the court balance the agency's need for secrecy with the plaintiff's right to challenge the evidence?

questions.title: Does an 'ongoing investigation' always qualify as a 'proceeding' under Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: The court references the case 'CREW' to say that ongoing criminal investigations count as 'proceedings' that are 'pending or reasonably anticipated.' However, usually, a 'proceeding' implies something formal, like a lawsuit or an indictment. If the FBI is just 'gathering evidence' without a formal charge, how is that a 'proceeding'? I'm struggling to find the line between a general investigation and a 'concrete prospective law enforcement proceeding.'

questions.title: What is the 'inextricably intertwined' standard for segregability in large record sets?
questions.question_body: The FBI withheld over 10,000 pages, claiming that non-exempt material was 'inextricably intertwined' or 'interspersed line-by-line' with exempt material. The court seems to accept that no 'meaningful information' was segregable. If a document is 10,000 pages long, is it practically possible for every single page to be so intertwined that not even a few sentences can be released? I'm trying to understand how high the bar is for the government to avoid the duty to segregate.

questions.title: How does 'deference' to the FBI impact the government's burden of proof under FOIA?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that the government bears the burden of showing that an exemption applies, but then immediately says that because the FBI specializes in law enforcement, its decisions are 'entitled to deference.' This feels contradictory. If the court defers to a 'terse' declaration (like Bender's) and accepts the agency's word that an investigation is still ongoing, hasn't the burden effectively shifted to the plaintiff to prove that the investigation is *not* ongoing?

questions.title: What does it mean for a FOIA withholding category to be 'overbroad'?
questions.question_body: In Section IV(C), the court mentions that when an agency withholds documents by category, those categories must be 'sufficiently distinct' so the court can determine if the exemption applies. Farahi argued the categories were overbroad, but the court said he 'forfeited' the argument because he didn't explain why. I don't understand what an 'overbroad category' looks like in practice. What is an example of a category that is 'sufficiently distinct' versus one that is too broad?
